content:
Many students know what they want to say in TOEFL Speaking but lose marks because they rush, mumble or freeze. The fix is not more vocabulary. It is a clear, steady voice that a listener can follow without effort. These TOEFL speaking tips focus on exactly that: fluency, pronunciation, pacing and a daily practice routine that builds confidence for the new TOEFL iBT format introduced in January 2026.

What the TOEFL Speaking section looks like now

Since 21 January 2026, the TOEFL iBT Speaking section is shorter and has two task types, taking about 8 minutes in total:

  • Listen and Repeat: you hear short sentences in a campus or academic setting and repeat each one exactly as you heard it. The sentences grow longer and more complex as you go.
  • Take an Interview: you answer a set of interview-style questions about your experiences and opinions, with prompts that move from simple facts to explanations and predictions.

Each response is scored out of 5, and the section is reported on the new 1 to 6 band scale. ETS describes what it measures in plain terms: intelligible speech, a natural speaking pace, and appropriate vocabulary and grammar. In other words, how you sound matters as much as what you say.

This post is about your voice. If you want ready-made answer frameworks for each task, read our companion guide on TOEFL speaking templates and response structure.

TOEFL speaking tips for a clearer voice

Pronunciation: aim to be understood, not to copy an accent

You do not need an American or British accent. The ETS descriptors at higher levels talk about being “fully intelligible with minimal listener effort”. For many Malayalam speakers, a few habits cause most of the trouble:

  • Word stress: saying “DE-ve-lop” instead of “de-VE-lop”, or “HO-tel” instead of “ho-TEL”. Wrong stress makes familiar words hard to recognise.
  • “V” and “W”: “very” and “worry” should sound different. Practise with your top teeth touching your lower lip for “v”.
  • Word endings: final “-ed” and “-s” sounds often disappear (“I walk there yesterday”). Dropping them also sounds like a grammar mistake.
  • Extra vowels: avoid adding a vowel at the start or end of a word, such as “is-school” for “school”.

Pick one habit a week and work on it deliberately. Trying to fix everything at once usually fixes nothing. Our trainers often point out that this single change makes other TOEFL speaking tips easier to apply.

Pacing: slower than you think

Nervous speakers speed up. A moderate, even pace sounds more fluent than a fast pace full of restarts. A useful check: if you cannot breathe comfortably between sentences, you are going too fast.

Intonation and stress: make meaning easy to follow

Stress the words that carry information and let small words stay light. “I prefer studying in the library because it’s quiet.” Let your voice fall at the end of a statement and rise slightly for a yes/no question. This is exactly what Listen and Repeat rewards at higher levels: rhythm and intonation that convey meaning.

Fluency: keep the sound flowing

Fluency is not speed. It is the absence of long gaps, repeated words and false starts. Two habits help:

  • Use short linking phrases such as “The main reason is …” or “For example …” to give yourself a second to think without going silent.
  • Do not correct small slips. Going back to fix one word interrupts your flow and usually costs more than the slip itself.

How to practise Listen and Repeat

This task tests how accurately you hold and reproduce spoken English. Practise it with real audio:

  1. Take a short clip from a university podcast, lecture or campus video.
  2. Pause after each sentence and repeat it aloud, copying the rhythm, stress and linking, not just the words.
  3. Record yourself and compare with the original. Where did you drop a word or change the stress?
  4. Gradually choose longer sentences with clauses (“The library, which opens at eight, will close early on Friday”).

Listening for chunks of meaning, rather than single words, makes long sentences much easier to remember.

A 20-minute daily practice routine

Minutes Activity Goal
0 to 3 Warm up: read a short paragraph aloud slowly, then at normal pace Relax your voice and set a steady pace
3 to 8 Shadowing: repeat sentences from a short academic clip Rhythm, stress and Listen and Repeat accuracy
8 to 15 Interview practice: answer three or four questions about study life, recording each answer Fluency and natural pace under time pressure
15 to 20 Review: listen back, note one pronunciation habit and one fluency issue Self-correction and a focus for tomorrow

Keep your recordings. Of all the TOEFL speaking tips here, this may be the most motivating: comparing week one with week four shows you real progress.

Building confidence for test day

Mock tests under real conditions

Practise the full Speaking section in one go, timed, with headphones and a microphone. The format is short, so the challenge is staying sharp from the first sentence to the last interview question.

Feedback from another listener

Self-recording shows you a lot, but another listener notices habits you cannot hear. Practise with a study partner, or better, with a trainer who knows what the scoring descriptors reward.

Handling nerves

  • Breathe out slowly before each response. A long exhale calms the voice.
  • Focus only on the current question, not on the one you just answered.
  • If you lose your idea, finish the sentence simply and add one more reason or example. Keep talking calmly.

Frequently asked questions

Does my Indian accent lower my TOEFL Speaking score?

No, an accent alone does not. What matters is intelligibility: clear sounds, correct word stress and natural rhythm. Many Indian speakers score highly with a clear Indian accent.

How long does it take to improve TOEFL speaking fluency?

It depends on your starting level, but daily practice of about 20 minutes usually produces noticeable change within a few weeks. Consistency matters more than long weekend sessions.

Is there preparation time in the new TOEFL Speaking tasks?

The new tasks are short and quick, so you will not get the long planning time of older TOEFL tasks. That is why fluency habits and a familiar answer structure matter so much. Check the official ETS practice materials before test day so the timing feels familiar.
